title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows a general-purpose AI coding and agent tool being used as an active component in a criminal intrusion campaign rather than for its intended development purposes. The Aurora ransomware group ran Cursor Agent, with Claude Sonnet as the underlying model, to conduct hands-on exploitation against target organizations. This is a case of a legitimate tool deployed outside the conditions it was designed for, specifically weaponized to assist in network compromise and ransomware deployment against ESXi environments.

The failure is one of misuse rather than model malfunction. The AI system functioned as designed, executing agentic tasks, but those tasks were offensive security operations directed at victim organizations. There is no indication in the reporting that the tool had safeguards sufficient to detect or interrupt this class of use. Catching this kind of abuse would require behavioral monitoring at the tool or platform level, capable of distinguishing exploitation workflows from ordinary development activity, a control that was evidently not present or not effective here.

What is not established is whether the tool's developers had knowledge of this use, whether any platform-level policies were triggered, and the full scope of harm across all named victim organizations, as the reporting reflects researcher findings rather than confirmed legal findings or verified victim disclosures.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team identified the Aurora ransomware group operating since April 2026, targeting organizations across multiple countries. The group developed a Linux variant of their ransomware capable of attacking ESXi virtualization environments. Between April 8 and May 21, 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent running Claude Sonnet to conduct hands-on exploitation against ten target organizations. The ESXi ransomware uses ChaCha20 encryption and includes a special mode to encrypt only virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands.

Researchers also discovered the Aurora group employed a custom tool called esxi_finder.py to scan networks for ESXi hosts and vCenter servers. A second cluster of suspected Aurora activity was identified in eight victim organizations across multiple countries, using different attack methods including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to S3 storage. The investigation revealed the attackers were careful to avoid certain actions like account lockouts and DCSync attacks, suggesting operational discipline within the group.
